seo.title: Hawaii Mini Semester | Pacific Discovery
seo.description: Hawaiʻi in 6 weeks: an Imu feast, Volcanoes National Park, manta rays, a permaculture farm, fishpond restoration, Mauna Kea and surf lessons on Oʻahu. Ages 17–22.

hero.headline: Six weeks across Hawaiʻi Island and Oʻahu
hero.intro: Cook an Imu feast in Pahala, snorkel with manta rays off Kona, stargaze from Mauna Kea, restore a fishpond in Hilo and learn to surf in Haleʻiwa.

itinerary.heading: Week by week
itinerary.note: This is a guide to what you can expect to do on program. The order in which activities occur might vary. Itineraries are subject to change.

weeks.title: Volcanoes & an Imu feast
weeks.body:
You’ll meet your Program Instructors in Hilo and drive to Pahala for orientation. From there we tour Volcanoes National Park, usually hiking the Kīlauea Iki Trail from the crater rim to the crater floor and back.

With our local host James we spend a full day building the imu pit, heating the stones and preparing the food, then return early the next morning to uncover it for our feast, followed by a musical performance. The week ends with the drive to the Kona side and our campsite at Hoʻokena.
weeks.imageAlt: Group preparing banana stalks and leaves beside a smoking fire pit

weeks.title: Manta rays & a permaculture farm
weeks.body:
From our camp at Hoʻokena we explore the Kona side of the island and head out on a manta ray boat tour to snorkel with the mantas.

Next we move to Big Island Farms near Honokaʻa and stay in the farm’s cabanas. A permaculture workshop introduces local farming techniques, a coconut workshop teaches us how to open coconuts and use every part, and a marine biology class looks at the coral reefs around the island, where we also make our own reef-safe sunscreen.

weeks.title: Voyaging canoes & ancient farming
weeks.body:
We harvest ingredients for a farm-to-table vegetarian meal, then move to Waipiʻo Lodge. Two days with Na Kalai Waʻa introduce traditional voyaging canoe observation and cultural practice, from a history walk at Puʻukoholā Heiau and a knot lesson to the history of Mahukona.

With Ulu Mau Puanui we learn how Hawaiians sustained rain-fed intensive farming for centuries. In Hilo we take a Hawaiian language introduction and cultural history session with Traven, then start restoring the Hale o Lono fishpond in Keaukaha, clearing debris and invasive plants and dry stacking stone walls.
weeks.imageAlt: Group of students holding buckets and litter grabbers on a sandy beach

weeks.title: Fishpond, Mauna Kea & first waves
weeks.body:
A second day at the fishpond covers wall repair, mākāhā (sluice gate) maintenance and limu (seaweed) propagation, ending with a closing ceremony. Then we head up Mauna Kea, a dormant volcano nearly 14,000 feet above sea level, to stargaze from the summit.

Morning yoga sessions and time to explore Hilo round out our time on Hawaiʻi Island. We fly to Honolulu, settle into Haleʻiwa and start our surf lessons with HI Surf.
weeks.imageAlt: Group in warm jackets standing under a starry night sky

weeks.title: Surf, snorkel & service on Oʻahu
weeks.body:
Two more days of surf lessons in Haleʻiwa build on the basics, and we snorkel at Shark Cove before a free day to explore.

In Honolulu we settle in at Sun Farm and spend an evening at the Bishop Museum’s Museum After Dark. Then come two days of service learning with Papahana, learning about habitat restoration and the island’s native and invasive species, and helping with invasive species removal.
weeks.imageAlt: Students lined up on a beach beside surfboards for a lesson

weeks.title: Food bank, Hanauma Bay & farewell
weeks.body:
We visit Lyon Arboretum and Mānoa Falls, then spend two mornings at the Hawaiʻi Food Bank sorting and boxing food for distribution. One evening we climb an old railway track up the rim of Koko Crater for sunset views over Oʻahu’s eastern coast.

We snorkel in Hanauma Bay, inside a volcanic crater on the southeast coast, and take a guided sea kayak tour to the Twin Islands with snorkeling and a marine conservation discussion. We finish with our program wrap and reflections before flying home from Honolulu.

notes.title: Free time
notes.body: Each week there is some designated free time to catch up on email and laundry, rest and explore with others in the group.

notes.title: Phones & wifi
notes.body: We encourage flight mode so you stay present. Wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns.

notes.title: Fitness needed
notes.body: Medium activity level. Anyone with average fitness and enthusiasm for the outdoors will be fine. Expect hiking, surfing, snorkeling and kayaking, and some physical work on volunteer projects such as fishpond restoration and invasive species removal.

items.title: Hawaiian culture & the land
items.body: Learn traditional voyaging canoe practice with Na Kalai Waʻa, take a Hawaiian language and cultural history session in Hilo, and learn how Hawaiians sustained rain-fed farming with Ulu Mau Puanui.

items.title: Optional college credit
items.body: Earn college credit through the University of Montana. 529 education funds can be used to pay for your credits and your Pacific Discovery program tuition.

faq.heading: Questions we get about this program

items.q: How fit do I need to be?
items.a: The program suits anyone of average fitness. Be ready for hikes like the Kīlauea Iki Trail (3–4 miles) and the steep climb up Koko Crater, plus surfing, snorkeling and kayaking. Volunteer projects also involve physical work, such as fishpond restoration and invasive species removal.

items.q: Do I need to know how to surf?
items.a: No. You’ll have three days of surf lessons with HI Surf in Haleʻiwa, and you don't need previous experience with any of the activities.
On our Hawaii programs there is a lot of student-led cooking. In small groups you plan, budget and cook for the others, with your instructors there to help with planning and recipes.
A mix of cottages, lodges and hostels, camping at Hoʻokena and in Hilo, cabanas at Big Island Farms and Sun Farm in Honolulu.

Tuition covers all in-country transport, accommodation, meals, and the activities and entry fees in the itinerary. It doesn't cover flights to and from Hawaiʻi, travel insurance, spending money, optional college credit or optional activities.

items.q: How much spending money should I bring?
items.a: About $100 a week for snacks, laundry, personal shopping and optional activities. It varies from student to student.

items.q: Can I stay in touch with home?
items.a: Yes. We encourage keeping phones on flight mode so you stay present, and wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns. There will also be a photo album that students and instructors can upload photos and video to, so parents and caregivers can stay up to date.

safety.heading: For parents: how we keep students safe

items.title: 24/7 Emergency Line
items.body: Parents, students and instructors can reach a real person at any hour. Every call is logged and passed to our on-call staff member by phone.

items.title: Wilderness First Aid & Live Risk Assessment
items.body: All our instructors hold Wilderness First Aid (WFA) certification and have extensive training in group leadership and risk management.

items.title: Accredited Safety Systems
items.body: Our safety systems are assessed and accredited by the Gap Year Association (USA), Year Out Group (UK) and OutdoorsMark (NZ). Students on Go Overseas voted us one of the top gap year providers for safety.

items.title: Insurance & Health
items.body: Comprehensive travel insurance is required, covering medical costs and emergency evacuation. Check vaccinations with your doctor, and pack a first-aid kit and any personal medication. Our instructors can't legally give students any medication.
